# THE HATEFUL IMMORTALS
## A Documentary History of the Greenbriar-Chen Marriage, 1847–2024

**By Dr. Amelia Thornton, PhD**
*Hawthorne Chair of Parahuman Studies, Columbia University*

*Published by Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2024*
*Winner of the National Book Award for Nonfiction*

---

## A Note on Sources

This history draws upon 4,216 letters exchanged between Margaret Greenbriar and James Chen (many written while living in the same house, during periods of "not speaking"); Margaret's personal recollections, which constitute—thanks to her total eidetic recall—the most comprehensive oral history archive any single human has ever produced; forty-six hours of interviews conducted by the author between 2019 and 2024; municipal records, immigration documents, and property deeds from fourteen countries; and one deeply unfortunate home video from 1987 that both parties asked me to destroy and neither party gave me legal authority to do so.

James Chen also provided what he described as his own "memory book," which turned out to be a water-damaged composition notebook containing approximately thirty pages of bullet-point notes covering the entirety of the twentieth century. The entry for 1969 reads, in full: "Moon. Woodstock. Margaret angry (reason unclear)."

Margaret, upon seeing this notebook during our joint interview session in Portland, closed her eyes for eleven seconds and then recited, from memory, the complete text of the argument of March 14, 1969, which lasted four hours and concerned James's failure to attend her naturalization ceremony for their Canadian identities because he had "lost track of which decade required which passport." She then noted that she had also been upset about the moon landing, because James had promised her in 1873 that he would take her to see "the next great impossible thing humanity accomplishes" and had instead spent July 20, 1969, asleep on a couch in Winnipeg.

James's response: "I was tired. I'd been alive for a hundred and forty-three years."

Margaret's response: "I had been alive for precisely the same amount of time, James."

This exchange, I came to learn, is essentially the Greenbriar-Chen marriage in miniature.

---

# PART ONE: CONVERGENCE (1847–1860)

---

## Chapter 1: Two Miracles in Boston

The story begins, as so many parahuman stories do, with two adolescents who had no idea what was happening to them.

Margaret Greenbriar was born on April 7, 1826, in Beacon Hill, Boston, the third daughter of Josiah Greenbriar, a moderately successful textile merchant, and his wife, Prudence née Alcott (no relation to the Concord Alcotts, a fact Prudence mentioned with considerable bitterness according to Margaret's recollection). She was, by all available accounts, an unremarkable girl—pleasant, literate, prone to daydreaming—until the spring of 1840, when she turned fourteen and the world became, in her words, "a room that would never again be cleaned."

"You must understand that before the change, I was ordinary in the most complete sense," Margaret told me during our first interview, seated in the living room of the Portland bookshop she and James have operated since 2015. "I forgot things. I lost things. I once left a glove in a church pew and did not think of it again for a week. Can you imagine? A whole week without a thought. I would give—" She paused here and looked at the ceiling. "I would give rather a lot, Dr. Thornton, to know what it feels like to forget a glove."

The onset of Margaret's total eidetic recall was not instantaneous. Over the course of approximately three months in 1840, her memory sharpened from normal to extraordinary to what she describes as "absolute." By her fifteenth birthday, she could recall every word of every conversation she had participated in or overheard since the change began. By sixteen, she had realized with mounting horror that the ability was not fading, not selective, and not controllable. Every sound, sight, smell, texture, and taste was being recorded in perfect fidelity, permanently, without her consent.

"People think it is a gift," she said. "People are idiots."

She said this with a brightness that suggested the observation brought her genuine satisfaction, even after 184 years.

James Chen was born on September 12, 1826, in the same city but a different universe—the cramped rooms above his father's laundry on Tyler Street, in what would later become Boston's Chinatown. His father, Chen Wei-Lin, had arrived in Boston in 1819, part of a small and largely invisible wave of Chinese immigration to the eastern seaboard that predated the Gold Rush migration by three decades. His mother, Mary Chen (née Mary Sullivan, of Galway, in a union that scandalized both families with admirable equality), had died in childbirth. James was raised by his father, two uncles, and the entire rotating population of the laundry's back rooms, a circumstance that left him, in Margaret's assessment, "pathologically comfortable with chaos and incapable of understanding that drawers exist for a reason."

James's ability manifested at thirteen with an incident that, in retrospect, should have killed him. In August of 1839, he fell from the roof of a three-story boarding house on Beach Street, where he had been attempting to retrieve a kite. He struck the cobblestones headfirst. Several witnesses reported hearing the unmistakable sound of skeletal fracture.

He stood up.

"Hurt like the devil," he told me, with the easy grin that Margaret has described, at various points across 177 years, as "charming," "infuriating," "the single most punchable expression in the Western Hemisphere," and—once, during a rare moment of unguarded tenderness I was not meant to overhear—"the first thing I ever wanted to memorize on purpose."

The full scope of James's ability would not become clear for several years. It was not simply durability, nor rapid healing, nor even conventional immortality. James Chen cannot be killed. He cannot be permanently injured. He has, across the span of his documented life, survived falls, stabbings, shootings, drowning, two building collapses, the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, a direct lightning strike (1923, Buenos Aires), influenza, tuberculosis, smallpox, what he believes was bubonic plague ("or a very bad sandwich, it was 1897, hard to say"), and, on one occasion in 1944, an actual bomb. His body repairs itself with a speed proportional to the severity of the injury—cuts close in seconds, broken bones set in minutes, and the bomb, which by all rights should have distributed him across a quarter-mile of French countryside, required approximately four hours of what he describes as "a deeply unpleasant nap."

He does not age. Neither, as it happens, does Margaret, though this was not immediately apparent—her aging slowed gradually beginning around age twenty-five and stopped entirely, as far as anyone can determine, sometime in the 1870s. The mechanism is unclear. Her ability is cognitive, not physical, and no satisfying explanation has been offered for why perfect memory should confer biological immortality. Margaret has her own theory.

"The universe," she told me, "has a depraved sense of humor."

---

## Chapter 2: A Courtship in the Proper Style

They met on October 3, 1847.

Margaret can tell you the weather (overcast, fifty-one degrees, wind from the northeast carrying the smell of low tide and roasting chestnuts). She can tell you what she was wearing (a brown wool dress with ivory buttons, the third button from the top slightly loose—"I had been meaning to fix it for a week; I never did; I can feel it now, that tiny wobble under my thumb"). She can tell you the exact angle of light through the window of Burnham's Bookshop on Washington Street, where she had gone to purchase a copy of Jane Eyre, newly published and scandalous.

She can tell you that James was wearing a blue cotton shirt with the sleeves rolled to the elbows, that there was a smear of ink on his left wrist, that he was reading a copy of the *North Star* that someone had left on the counter, and that when he looked up at her, his eyes were so dark they appeared to contain no pupils at all.

"He smiled at me," Margaret recalled. "I am aware that this is not, in the general course of human events, a remarkable thing. People smile at each other. But I must tell you that I had been living for seven years inside a memory that never stopped recording, never stopped accumulating, and everything was noise. Everything was *everything*, all the time, without relief. And when he smiled at me—"

She stopped. She looked at the window.

"It was the first time since the change that I wanted to remember something. That I was glad I would."

James's recollection of their first meeting, as recorded in his composition notebook, reads: "Met M. at a bookshop. Pretty."

I showed this to Margaret. She said, "Yes, that is exactly the level of emotional detail I have come to expect from a man who once described our wedding as 'nice, I think.'"

---

Their courtship lasted approximately eighteen months, which was slightly long by the standards of their era and, as Margaret points out, represents less than one percent of the time they have subsequently spent arguing about whose turn it is to reinvent their identities for a new city.

The courtship was complicated by factors that would have been insurmountable for most couples in 1847 Boston. James was half-Chinese, half-Irish, and fully poor. Margaret was the daughter of a respectable Anglo-Saxon merchant. The social chasm between them was vast, and the racial prejudice James faced was constant, grinding, and, in Margaret's recollection, breathtakingly casual.

"I remember," Margaret said during one of our interviews, "every single word anyone ever said to James or about James in my presence regarding his race. Every word. I remember the woman at the dressmaker's who saw us walking together and said—" She recited a slur that I will not reproduce here, then paused. "I remember the exact pitch of her voice. The color of her bonnet. The fact that she had a crumb of something—I believe it was pound cake—at the corner of her lip. I remember that James's hand tightened on my arm for exactly one second and then relaxed, and that he kept walking, and that he said, very quietly, 'It doesn't matter,' and I knew even then that he had heard this word so many times it had become weather. Background rain. And I remember thinking: I will never let this be weather. I will remember every instance. I will keep count."

She has. The count, as of our final interview in March 2024, stands at 14,7093.

"James thinks the number is morbid," she said. "James thinks I should let some things go. James has the luxury of forgetting."

"I don't think it's morbid," James said from the other room, apparently having been eavesdropping. "I think it's—I mean, it's a little morbid, Maggie."

"Don't call me Maggie."

"You liked it in 1953."

"I *tolerated* it in 1953, and only because we were in Florence and the wine was exceptional and you were being less irritating than usual."

"See, that's what I love about you. The warmth."

Despite these obstacles, they persisted. James, it should be noted, was not destitute—he had, by 1847, leveraged his apparent indestructibility into reliable employment at the dockyards, where his willingness to perform the most dangerous tasks without injury made him simultaneously invaluable and unsettling to his coworkers. Margaret, for her part, had begun to quietly establish herself as an invaluable resource for Boston's legal community, her perfect recall of contracts, testimony, and precedent making her an unofficial—and, given her gender, unacknowledged—asset to several prominent attorneys.

They were, in other words, two people with impossible abilities trying to lead ordinary lives in a world that did not yet have a vocabulary for what they were. They found in each other the only person who understood.

"He was the only one who didn't flinch," Margaret said. "When I told him what I could do—when I demonstrated it, when I recited to him the entirety of a conversation we had shared three months prior, word for word, including his pauses and the exact moment he had scratched his left eyebrow—he did not flinch. He said, 'That must be exhausting.' And he was right. He was right, and he was the first person to say it."

James, asked what had drawn him to Margaret, said: "She remembered me. Not just—she *remembered* me. Every version of me, from the first second. Do you know what that's like, to be known that completely? It's terrifying. I loved it immediately."

This, it turned out, was both the foundation of their marriage and the source of its most enduring agony: Margaret would remember everything, and James would live through everything, and neither of them would ever be able to escape the accumulated weight of a shared life that refused to end.

---

## Chapter 3: The Wedding and the Vow

They married on June 15, 1849, in a small ceremony in the parlor of a sympathetic Unitarian minister named Reverend Elias Whitcomb, who was either admirably progressive or deeply unobservant regarding the racial dynamics of the union he was sanctifying. Present were Margaret's youngest sister, Anne (the only family member still speaking to her); James's father, Wei-Lin; and a dock worker named Thomas Flannery, who served as witness and, according to Margaret, spent the entire ceremony examining a callus on his left hand.

Margaret remembers the vows. She recited them for me in full. I will reproduce here only the minister's traditional closing, which has become, in light of subsequent events, one of history's great unintentional cruelties:

*"Till death do us part."*

"He said it so *confidently*," Margaret observed. "As though death were a reliable institution. As though it were the post office. I trusted him. The minister, I mean. I trusted that death would come and do its part. Death, it turns out, is derelict in its duties."

James's recollection of the wedding, from his notebook: "Married M. Hot day. Cake was good."

---

The first three years of the marriage were, by Margaret's account, genuinely happy. They rented rooms on Myrtle Street. James worked the docks; Margaret took in copying work, her perfect memory allowing her to reproduce documents with mechanical accuracy. They were poor but not destitute, in love but not naive, and possessed of a shared private world in which their abilities were not secrets to be hidden but facts to be lived with, together.

"We were extraordinary together," Margaret told me, in one of the rare moments when her voice lost its cultivated tartness. "Do you understand? In the world, we were freaks. Anomalies. But in our rooms on Myrtle Street, we were simply—us. He would come home smelling of salt and tar, and I would tell him every detail of my day, knowing he could not retain half of it, and he would listen with this—this *expression*—as though I were narrating something wonderful instead of recounting the tedium of copying legal briefs. And at night, we would lie in the dark, and I would describe to him the exact color of the sky on the evening we met, and he would say, 'Are you sure it wasn't bluer?' and I would say, 'James, I am literally incapable of being wrong about this,' and he would say, 'But what if it *felt* bluer?' and—"

She stopped.

"He was infuriating," she said. "He has always been infuriating. He made me laugh."
